props.title: Crossing Delancey

sections.content: Crossing Delancey (1988) brilliantly captures the cultural tensions of late-1980s Manhattan, where traditional Jewish values collide with contemporary urban life. Amy Irving shines as Isabelle "Izzy" Grossman, a sophisticated bookstore employee torn between Sam (Peter Riegert), the humble pickle vendor set up by her grandmother's matchmaker, and Anton (Jeroen Krabbé), a pretentious author representing her aspirational literary world. The film shares DNA with Moonstruck (1987) and When Harry Met Sally (1989) in its authentic portrayal of ethnic New York romance, but director Joan Micklin Silver brings a distinctly feminine and Jewish perspective rarely seen in mainstream cinema of the era.

sections.content: The film stands as a crucial entry in the canon of Jewish-American cinema, alongside earlier works like The Jazz Singer (1927) and later films like A Serious Man (2009). What sets Crossing Delancey apart is its nuanced exploration of assimilation versus tradition without demonizing either side. The Lower East Side setting becomes a character itself, with Riegert's pickle shop representing a vanishing world of immigrant Jewish culture while Irving's Upper West Side bookstore embodies secular modernity.

Director Joan Micklin Silver, who previously helmed Hester Street (1975), brings remarkable authenticity to the material, treating the matchmaker (Sylvia Miles) and grandmother (Reizl Bozyk) with dignity rather than as cultural caricatures. The film's lasting influence can be seen in later works like Keep the Change (2017) and Arranged (2007), which similarly explore the intersection of traditional matchmaking and modern romance. sections.content: While Annie Hall (1977) approached Jewish identity through Woody Allen's neurotic lens, Crossing Delancey offers a female perspective on cultural preservation versus assimilation. The film's exploration of generational differences and dating expectations resonates with later works like Two Lovers (2008) and Obvious Child (2014), showing how Jewish filmmakers continue examining identity in an increasingly secular world.
